description_full: American Assets Trust, Inc. is a full service, vertically integrated and self-administered real estate investment trust. The company has over 55 years of experience in acquiring, improving, developing and managing premier office, retail, and residential properties throughout the United States in some of the nations most dynamic, high-barrier-to-entry markets primarily in Southern California, Northern California, Washington, Oregon, Texas and Hawaii. Its office portfolio comprises approximately 4.3 million rentable square feet, and its retail portfolio comprises approximately 2.4 million rentable square feet. In addition, the company owns one mixed-use property (including approximately 94,000 rentable square feet of retail space and a 369-room all-suite hotel) and 2,302 multifamily units. In 2011, the company was formed to succeed to the real estate business of American Assets, Inc., a privately held corporation founded in 1967 and, as such, has significant experience, long-standing relationships and extensive knowledge of its core markets, submarkets and asset classes. American Assets Trust, Inc. is headquartered in San Diego, California. American Assets Trust, Inc. was incorporated in 1967 in Maryland and based in San Diego, California.

financial_summary: American Assets Trust, Inc. is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.7B market cap on $436M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 64% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $95M in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.00× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.7× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Value-trap profile (score 57/100): leveraged balance sheet under pressure; durably derated by the market — cheapness may reflect deterioration, not mispricing
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 33% operating margin runs 11pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.69x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 0.83, it moves roughly with the market.
About $8.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash and 36% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 48% below its DCF fair value of $41.75, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 62%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $29.35 to $58.92 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 12.3 vs 16.2, richer on P/E 62.0 vs 23.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 43% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $23.50 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It runs a 64% gross margin and converts 22% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.00x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 22%.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.7x net debt to EBITDA ($129.4M of cash against $1.7B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.71 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.1% over 3 years, 4.8% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 8.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 5.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (16.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.8%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (24 purchases, net $21.3M bought).
It returns 6.3% a year to shareholders (6.3% in dividends).
It pays out 389% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 228 employees, each generates about $1.9M of revenue, 0.8x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 5.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $416K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
